proposals.butler: making him look taller and stouter than he really was
proposals.reader_evidence: Barrier (pause, medium) on 'taller and stouter': 'Bigger and more powerfully built, not fatter'. Note: "modern 'stout' means plump".
proposals.reason: Of a person, current 'stout' chiefly means portly, so a typical reader has Athena make Odysseus fatter while she 'beautifies' him for athletic trials. Butler's sense is strong and solidly built (Greek passona, 'thicker, sturdier', Od. 8.20). 'Sturdier' keeps his meaning and his comparative. 'Stout' stays where it is current, in 'good stout clothing' at 7.21; that split by referent is to be recorded.
proposals.collision_check: Butler ¶1: flocked, seats, standing room, struck, appearance, beautified, head, shoulders, taller, stouter, impress, favourably, remarkable, trials of skill, challenge. 'Sturdy' occurs nowhere in Butler's Books 7–8.

proposals.quote_modern: I will find you in everything.
proposals.replacement: I will supply you with everything.
proposals.butler: I will find you in everything.
proposals.reader_evidence: Barrier (unsure, medium; 'archaic') on 'I will find you in everything': "I will provide everything you need (food and drink), not 'I will come and find you'." book_level lists it among the archaic idioms.
proposals.reason: An obsolete sense of 'find': to supply someone with something, as in 'all found'. Current English reads it as 'I will come and find you', or cannot read it, and the reader had to guess. The sense matters, because the king is undertaking to provide the feast (Greek pasi parexo, Od. 8.39, 'I will provide for all'). 'Supply ... with' is the plain current verb for Butler's sense. The change also removes a second, different 'find' from a paragraph that opens with 'has found his way'.
proposals.collision_check: Butler ¶2: found (his way, = reached), ready (get one ready), prepare (a feast), find (= supply). 'Supply' occurs nowhere in Butler's Book 8. 'Provide' was rejected: Butler uses it at 8.3 ('so as to provide a magnificent banquet'), so one rendering would serve two Butler words (arrow B). 'Prepare' and 'ready' are Butler's words here for other things.

proposals.quote_modern: and Alcinous killed them a dozen sheep
proposals.replacement: and for them Alcinous killed a dozen sheep
proposals.butler: and Alcinous killed them a dozen sheep, eight full grown pigs, and two oxen
proposals.reader_evidence: Barrier (pause, high; syntax) on 'Alcinous killed them a dozen sheep': "first pass reads 'killed them', i.e. the men".
proposals.reason: An indirect object without 'for' after 'killed' is obsolete. Coming straight after 'crowds of men ... both old and young', it first reads as the king killing the crowd, the kind of syntax that hides who is done to. Moving 'them' into a 'for' phrase at the head of the clause (the Greek order, toisin d' Alkinoos, Od. 8.59) keeps every word and leaves the list intact.
proposals.collision_check: No new content word; all of Butler's words in ¶3 are kept. 'For' is a function word.

proposals.butler: when we Achaeans were before Troy and in practice
proposals.reader_evidence: Barrier (pause, medium) on 'when we Achaeans were before Troy and in practice': "'and in practice' is unclear (shooting practice as opposed to battle?)".
proposals.reason: 'In practice' is now a fixed idiom for 'in reality', so the qualifier reads as nonsense or as a hedge. Butler means when the Achaeans were practising archery (Greek hote toxazoimeth' Achaioi, Od. 8.220, 'when we Achaeans shot'). 'At practice' keeps Butler's noun and changes only the preposition. 'Before Troy' (= at the siege) was decoded and is kept, here and at 8.49.
proposals.collision_check: Butler uses 'practice' only here in ¶15; the change is to the preposition alone.

proposals.quote_modern: I can throw a dart farther
proposals.replacement: I can throw a spear farther
proposals.butler: I can throw a dart farther than any one else can shoot an arrow
proposals.reader_evidence: Barrier (pause, medium) on 'I can throw a dart farther than anyone else can shoot an arrow': "'dart' = a light throwing spear or javelin, not a small darts-board dart".
proposals.reason: Current 'dart' is the small missile of the pub game, which makes the boast absurd. Butler's 'dart' is the old word for a light spear (Greek douri akontizo, Od. 8.229, 'I hurl a spear'). 'Spear' is the plain current word for the object, and the object itself is kept.
proposals.collision_check: Butler ¶15: archer, arrow, shoot, disc, throw, dart. Neither 'spear' nor 'javelin' occurs in Butler's Book 8. 'Throw' is kept as Butler's verb.

proposals.quote_modern: Let us go to the couch of Hephaestus
proposals.replacement: Let us go to the bed of Hephaestus
proposals.butler: Let us go to the couch of Vulcan
proposals.reader_evidence: Barrier (pause, high) on 'the couch of Hephaestus': "Hephaestus's bed, not a sofa" ('recurs ¶20'). book_level lists 'couch' (bed) among older meanings that clash with modern ones.
proposals.reason: To a present-day reader a couch is a sofa. The lay turns on the bed that Hephaestus has netted with chains ('marriage bed', 'bedposts', 'all over the bed', 8.18). If the lovers go to a 'couch', the trap they fall into is on the wrong piece of furniture. Butler's couch is that bed (Greek lektronde, Od. 8.292). Accepted Book 3 made the same change ('Nestor left his couch' → 'left his bed', 3.31); Dawn's formulaic couch at 5.0 is a different case and stays. Apply together with B08-08 or not at all.
proposals.collision_check: Butler ¶19 has no 'bed'. Across the lay, Butler's 'couch' (8.19, 8.20) and 'bed' (8.18, 8.21) name one object (Greek lektron, demnia), so merging them is arrow B in form only, the same merge accepted at 3.31. If the lead applies arrow B strictly, reject B08-06 and B08-08 together.

proposals.replacement: She was not at all reluctant
proposals.reader_evidence: Barrier (pause, high) on 'She was nothing loath': 'She was entirely willing'. Note: "archaic; easily confused with 'loathe'". book_level lists 'nothing loath' among the archaic idioms.
proposals.reason: GLOSSARY rules this construction dead ('Loth/loath is dead in this construction') and fixes a replacement that this paragraph never received; the brief's sweep list names it too. Read as 'loathe', it blurs or inverts whether Aphrodite consents, and her willingness is the point of the lay. 'Not at all reluctant' is the literal modernization (nothing → not at all, loth → reluctant) and keeps Butler's litotes (Greek aspaston eeisato, Od. 8.295, 'it seemed welcome to her'). The Glossary's form is 'willingly enough', and Book 3's current text prints 'readily enough' (3.36). In Book 8 both collide with Butler's own words (see collision_check), so the lead should update the Glossary row to record the forms in use.
proposals.collision_check: Butler ¶20: loth, couch, rest, toils, cunning, spread, trap, turned back, scout, passion, vestibule. 'Reluctant' occurs nowhere in Butler's Book 8. 'Willing' (8.16, 'you are willing to show your prowess') and 'ready' (8.2, 'get one ready') are Butler's own words elsewhere in the Book (arrow B), which rules out 'willing(ly) enough' and 'ready/readily enough' here.

proposals.butler: so they went to the couch to take their rest
proposals.reader_evidence: The barrier on 'the couch of Hephaestus' at ¶19 ('recurs ¶20'); see B08-06.
proposals.reason: The companion of B08-06, in the sentence where the trap springs. Butler's 'couch' here renders demnia, the same Greek word as his 'bed' at 8.21 ('asleep on my bed'). Apply together with B08-06 or not at all.
proposals.collision_check: As for B08-06. Butler ¶20 has no 'bed'.

proposals.butler: they were caught in the toils which cunning Vulcan had spread for them
proposals.reader_evidence: Barrier (pause, high) on 'caught in the toils': "Caught in the net or snare of chains ('toils' = nets, not hard work)".
proposals.reason: 'Toils' in the sense of a net or snare is dead outside the literary idiom 'in the toils of'. The current 'toils' (labors) makes 'caught in the toils ... spread for them' momentarily unreadable. 'Net' names Butler's object, the chains hung 'like cobwebs' (8.18) and spread over the bed. Accepted Book 4 made exactly this change ('a lioness caught in the toils' → 'caught in a net', 4.72).
proposals.collision_check: Butler ¶20: toils, spread, trap ('found too late that they were in a trap'). 'Net' occurs nowhere in Butler's Book 8. 'Snare' was rejected because it is Butler's own word for the same device at 8.18 (arrow B), and 'trap' is Butler's in this same sentence.

proposals.butler: the sum I gave him for his baggage of a daughter, who is fair but not honest
proposals.reader_evidence: Barrier (unsure, medium; 'archaic insult') on 'his baggage of a daughter': 'An insult: a shameless or worthless woman, not luggage.' book_level: "'baggage' (a loose woman)".
proposals.reason: The sense of 'baggage' as a disreputable woman is obsolete. Today the word means luggage or 'emotional baggage', so the insult blurs into 'burdensome'. What Hephaestus says is that his wife is shameless (Greek kunopidos, Od. 8.319, 'dog-eyed', i.e. shameless). 'Hussy' is the current, if dated, word for exactly Butler's sense. It keeps his 'his X of a daughter' construction and his comic, bitter register.
proposals.collision_check: Butler ¶21: dishonouring, lame, handsome, clean built, cripple, parents, begotten, pair, bed, furious, fond, sum, baggage, daughter, fair, honest. 'Hussy' occurs nowhere in Butler's Book 8.

proposals.quote_modern: He had done so before an upper servant told him
proposals.replacement: He had done so by the time an upper servant told him
proposals.butler: He had done so before an upper servant told him to come to the bath and wash himself.
proposals.reader_evidence: Barrier (pause, medium; syntax) on 'He had done so before an upper servant told him': "it can first read as 'he had done this before, on an earlier occasion'".
proposals.reason: Straight after 'a knot that Circe had taught him', 'He had done so before' reads first as the idiom 'on earlier occasions'. This garden path hides the sequence Butler states: the knot was finished, then came the call to the bath. 'By the time' states Butler's relation exactly (he had finished when he was called) and adds nothing. It does not reintroduce v1's 'hardly', which round 1 removed as a change of sense (Book 8 continuity §5b, B08-P042 = p41).
proposals.collision_check: Butler ¶41: done (so), before, upper servant, remained, done (washing). 'Time' does not occur in Butler's ¶41. 'Finished' was avoided because it is Butler's own word at 8.18 ('finished his snare').

summary: Book 8 reads well: the reader's 50 paraphrases contain no story error, and 73 of the 80 barriers are pauses, mostly on Trojan-war background, custom (bride-price, surety, drink offerings) and the Butlerisms the package keeps on record (aldermen and town councilors, father stranger, cast in heavy damages, the bond proverb, guardian angel). The real problem type is a dead sense or false friend in a single word, concentrated in the lay of Ares and Aphrodite; two repairs are recommended: 'I will find you in everything' (8.2, an obsolete 'find' = supply, which the reader had to guess) and 'nothing loath' (8.20), where a GLOSSARY replacement was never applied. Nine optional repairs replace 'stouter', 'dart', 'in practice', 'couch' (twice), 'toils' and 'baggage' and untangle two garden paths ('killed them a dozen sheep', 'He had done so before'); couch → bed and toils → net follow accepted Books 3 and 4. The other candidate false friends (escort, copper, tripod, talent, joint, pilots, ransom, kept no blind lookout, a bad man's bond) are decoded in context and kept. Outside comprehension scope, noted but not proposed: 8.49 keeps the doubled 'tell me, and tell me truly' where GLOSSARY R6 fixes 'tell me truly'; Butler's sentential 'whereon' appears as 'whereupon' (8.17) and 'and' (8.22, 8.39), not GLOSSARY's 'at that'; and 'full grown' (8.3) and 'finer looking' (8.13, beside 'best-looking' at 8.7) are open where D15's standard is hyphenated. Paragraph numbers are the 0-based p of the pairs files; B0N-Pnnn IDs are 1-based.
